demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Threat.value: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
Being superalert or watchful or on guard
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

issues.item: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
issues.explanation: For trauma involving the unexpected death of a loved one, a specific sense of danger from strangers is hard to reconcile unless there is additional trauma history not represented here. The other threat items reflect generalized hypervigilance, but this item implies an interpersonal-danger context that is not supported by the trauma type or by any trigger, memory, appraisal, or strategy items.

issues.item: Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
issues.explanation: For trauma involving the unexpected death of a loved one, this threat profile is hard to reconcile clinically: all selected items imply persistent fear of immediate external physical danger, which fits assault/combat more than bereavement trauma. In isolation, bereavement-related PTSD can involve arousal, but a purely danger-scanning threat node without any accompanying memory, trigger, appraisal, or strategy content linking the threat to reminders of the loved one's death is not coherent here. This is also difficult to square with the formulation, which specifies no active edges; the threat items strongly imply linkage to triggers or trauma reminders, yet no such connected content is present.

vignette:
Lina, a 31-year-old journalist, first sought help after nearly two years of living with a pervasive, unsettling unease that had only intensified since her divorce. The turning point in her life, the event that cast a long shadow, was the sudden death of her younger sister, Maya. Maya, only 23, had been killed instantly in a hit-and-run accident on her way home from work. Lina, reporting on a local political rally that evening, had received the call from a frantic police officer. The details she later pieced together from police reports and news coverage — the mangled car, the anonymous driver who fled the scene — solidified a sense of brutal randomness and profound injustice.

In the months that followed, Lina found herself consumed by an overwhelming sense of guilt. She would replay moments from their last conversation, searching for anything she could have done differently, any warning she might have missed. A profound fear often washed over her, a chilling reminder of how quickly life could be snatched away. These strong negative feelings, a mixture of horror, anger, and deep shame for not having protected Maya, seemed to well up inside her without warning.

As time progressed, Lina noticed a constant state of hypervigilance had become her default. As a journalist, she was often out in the field, navigating busy city streets or interviewing sources in unfamiliar locations. She found herself constantly scanning her surroundings, her eyes darting to every car, every pedestrian, every shadow, as if expecting danger to materialize at any moment. The slightest unexpected noise – a car backfiring, a sudden shout from across the street – would cause her to jump, her heart pounding in her chest. She was perpetually on guard, her senses heightened to an exhausting degree.

Even in the perceived safety of her own apartment, a quiet refuge in the bustling heart of the city, Lina found herself unable to relax. She would try to unwind after a long day of chasing stories, perhaps by reading a book or watching a film, but her body remained tense, her mind racing. The feeling was a constant hum beneath the surface, preventing any true sense of calm or peace. She knew, intellectually, that her apartment was safe, yet the profound inability to let down her guard persisted, making sleep elusive and rest an alien concept. This ceaseless internal tension permeated every aspect of her life.

Her job, which once provided a sense of purpose and connection to the world, now felt like another arena where her heightened state of alert was both a burden and a necessary evil. She was always watching, always listening, always prepared for the worst. This vigilant posture was not something she could turn off. Her inability to relax meant that genuine connection with others felt increasingly difficult. She had recently started to consider whether this pervasive internal tension was why her marriage had ultimately fractured, leaving her feeling even more isolated. She found her constant state of watchfulness made her feel apart from others, always on guard even when she longed for closeness. The intense negative emotions continued to resurface, particularly when she encountered stories of other unexpected tragedies, bringing fresh waves of fear and anger about Maya’s fate. Lina presented for therapy, exhausted and desperate for an understanding of why she couldn’t simply "get over" what had happened, and why the world still felt so perpetually dangerous.
